analysis.one_liner: Would let corporations and unions pay for candidate-focused campaign ads from their treasuries, with no disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 75 cosponsors but never got a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal three core pieces of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 (the "McCain-Feingold" law): the rule that groups filing for "electioneering communications" must report those spending to the Federal Election Commission, the ban on corporations and labor unions paying for such ads out of their general treasury funds, and the rule treating ads coordinated with a candidate's campaign as campaign contributions. The repeal would apply retroactively to spending on or after November 6, 2002. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations would gain the most: they could again use general treasury money — shareholder funds — to run broadcast ads that name federal candidates right before elections, and no longer have to report those disbursements to the FEC. Labor unions would get the same freedom, though unions historically spend far less on broadcast ads. Wealthy individuals and outside groups would also benefit, since coordination with candidate campaigns would no longer count as a regulated contribution. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations and unions funding election ads

how_it_helps.text: Lifts the ban on corporations and labor organizations making electioneering communications — broadcast ads that name a federal candidate close to an election — so both could pay for them directly from general treasury funds rather than regulated political action committees.

Ends the FEC disclosure requirement for electioneering-communication spending, terminating reporting for any disbursement made on or after November 6, 2002, so the public would no longer learn who paid for these ads.
Removes the rule treating communications coordinated with a candidate's campaign as contributions, loosening the main legal check on outside groups working with campaign staff.
Sponsors framed the repeal as restoring free-speech rights, naming the bill the "First Amendment Restoration Act."

analysis.who_pays: Voters would pay with transparency: no reports would reveal who was funding the flood of candidate-naming ads in the final weeks of campaigns. Candidates and parties would face unregulated, undisclosed outside spending, and the FEC would lose its coordination rules as an enforcement tool. Ordinary citizens' practical ability to trace money in elections would shrink. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters, who lose disclosure of ad funders

drawbacks.text: Repealing the disclosure requirement means voters would have no way to know which corporations, unions, or individuals were paying for ads attacking or promoting candidates in the weeks before an election.

Lifting the treasury-funds ban would let corporate managements spend shareholder money on electioneering ads without any contribution limits or public accounting, and would remove the rule that ads coordinated with a candidate count as contributions.
The repeal would apply retroactively to spending on or after November 6, 2002, unwinding rules that had already taken effect under the 2002 law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit is restoring what sponsors see as unrestricted speech for corporations and unions. The cost is the loss of both the spending ban and the disclosure requirement — the two tools Congress had just used in 2002 to keep corporate and union treasury money out of candidate elections. Because the bill removes transparency at the same time it removes limits, even a supporter of looser campaign rules would have to acknowledge that voters would be left with no record of who is financing election-season advertising. The bill offered no replacement disclosure mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Roscoe Bartlett introduced the bill on February 11, 2004, with 12 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration.
The bill eventually attracted 75 cosponsors — 72 Republicans and 3 Democrats — but the committee took no action on it.
The complete action history shows no activity after the referral, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voters kept the disclosure requirement and the ban on corporate and union treasury spending for candidate-naming election ads, since the restrictions the bill targeted stayed in force. The corporations and unions that would have gained new spending rights got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, but 72 of the bill's 75 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 3 Democrats signing on.

industries.note: The bill would let corporations pay for broadcast ads naming federal candidates out of general treasury funds and would end the reporting requirement for those disbursements. The industry's gain — undisclosed spending on elections — comes directly at the cost of the public's ability to trace campaign money.

Unions would get the same right as corporations to spend treasury funds on electioneering communications and to stop reporting them. In practice, unions' electioneering budgets are far smaller than corporate ones, so the practical effect would be much smaller.

Removing the limits and disclosure rules would tend to increase the volume of electioneering ads, which is paid television time for broadcasters and ad buyers. The industry neither wins nor loses on the substance of the rules; it profits from whatever spending follows.
